description: Desarrollamos una plataforma de entrenamiento para jóvenes astronautas que combina aprendizaje, simulación y exploración espacial. Nuestra misión es inspirar a las futuras generaciones mediante experiencias educativas interactivas basadas en desafíos reales de las misiones de la NASA.
summary:
Junior Lunar Trainer is a free browser game, in English and Spanish, where kids aged 7 to 12 run a lunar outpost for five days. Players walk between modules, solve quick mini-games (reconnect power, close valves, align shield panels) and then make a choice where nothing is free: send energy to Air or to Shield, run the greenhouse at full power or save energy, shelter from a solar storm or keep working.

Air, Energy and Shield do not reset between days, so today's decision shapes tomorrow's risk. Solar flare and particle-storm alerts are built from archived NASA DONKI space weather records, verified by our team, and appear on a NASA data card with the source and date. Costs, drain rates and shield protection are game balance, not NASA measurements, and the game says so on its Sources screen.

No download or account is needed. It teaches the core engineering idea behind real missions: limited resources, competing needs, and consequences that accumulate over time.
details:
WHAT IT DOES
 Junior Lunar Trainer is a 2D top-down mission-control game. Over five "days" the player keeps a lunar outpost running by managing three resources: Air, Energy and Shield. Each day has missions at stations around the base. Each mission is a short mini-game (wiring nodes, closing valves in flow order, aligning shield panels) followed by a choice with visible costs. Events interrupt the day: a water leak, a power outage and solar storms where the player must decide between sheltering and continuing to work.

HOW IT TEACHES

  • No choice is free: every option shows its costs before the player confirms.
  • Resources carry over between days, so decisions accumulate.
  • Doing nothing fails; doing everything perfectly still leaves little margin.
  • A failed day is not a game over: the next day starts with less margin, and Mission Control helps after repeated failures.
  • A final report shows the player's hardest decisions and their costs.

CHALLENGE QUESTIONS
 Problem: space STEM content is often too abstract or too advanced; kids rarely see the trade-offs behind a mission.
 User: children aged 7 to 12, also usable with siblings, parents or in classrooms.
 Learning: resources are limited and shared, today's choices affect tomorrow, and protecting something always costs something else.
 NASA data: archived NASA DONKI solar flare (FLR) and solar energetic particle (SEP) records, curated locally and shown with source, date and an "archive data" label. Not presented as live.
 Mechanics: resource management with mini-games, costed choices, carry-over between days, events, and a replayable week selection.
 Team: Paulo – educational design & narrative; Diego – programming & systems; Bonifacio – NASA data curation & science; Josue – accessibility, testing & demo.

DATA HONESTY
 The game makes no network calls. NASA event data is packaged locally and always labeled as archive data with its consultation date. Game costs, drain rates and shield protection are game balance and are not NASA measurements. This is stated in the game's Sources screen. This is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

TOOLS
 TypeScript, Phaser 3, Vite, Vitest. All graphics are drawn by code and all sounds are synthesized by code; no external images or audio files.

CREATIVITY
 Kid-friendly mission-control gameplay where costs are visible before every decision, bilingual (ES/EN), accessible (keyboard, touch, large text, reduced motion), and playable without installing anything.
